questions.stem: The CD4+ Th1 cell activates the macrophage via CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. What is the principal antimicrobial consequence of this activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgE class switching in B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct antibody-mediated pore formation in bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enhanced killing of phagocytosed intracellular microbes via reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide

explanation.summary: Th1 cells license macrophages through CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. The activated ('classically activated') macrophage generates ROS and NO to kill ingested microbes, secretes TNF/IL-1/IL-12, and upregulates MHC and B7.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th1 cells license macrophages through CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. The activated ('classically activated') macrophage generates ROS and NO to kill ingested microbes, secretes TNF/IL-1/IL-12, and upregulates MHC and B7.

questions.stem: This figure summarizes diverse processes across NK, T, B, dendritic, and neutrophil cells: immune synapse formation, perforin/granule localization, phagocytic cup formation, podosome assembly, membrane protrusion, and migration. All of these depend on dynamic remodeling of which cellular structure?

explanation.summary: Actin polymerization/remodeling underlies immune-synapse formation, phagocytosis, granule delivery, podosome and membrane-protrusion dynamics, and leukocyte migration. Defects in actin regulators (e.g., WASP in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome) impair these functions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Actin polymerization/remodeling underlies immune-synapse formation, phagocytosis, granule delivery, podosome and membrane-protrusion dynamics, and leukocyte migration. Defects in actin regulators (e.g., WASP in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome) impair these functions.

questions.stem: This diagram shows glucocorticoids inhibiting NF-kB. What is the principal immunologic consequence of blocking this transcription factor?

explanation.summary: NF-kB drives transcription of many pro-inflammatory genes (cytokines, adhesion molecules, enzymes). By inhibiting NF-kB, glucocorticoids reduce inflammatory cytokine production, which accounts for much of their anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: NF-kB drives transcription of many pro-inflammatory genes (cytokines, adhesion molecules, enzymes). By inhibiting NF-kB, glucocorticoids reduce inflammatory cytokine production, which accounts for much of their anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effect.

questions.stem: In this hematopoiesis scheme, natural killer cells arise from a progenitor they share with which other cells?

choices.label: D
choices.text: T cells and B cells (the common lymphoid lineage)

explanation.summary: The hematopoietic stem cell gives rise to myeloid and lymphoid progenitors. The lymphoid progenitor produces T cells, B cells, and NK cells, whereas granulocytes, monocytes, erythrocytes, and platelets derive from the myeloid progenitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hematopoietic stem cell gives rise to myeloid and lymphoid progenitors. The lymphoid progenitor produces T cells, B cells, and NK cells, whereas granulocytes, monocytes, erythrocytes, and platelets derive from the myeloid progenitor.

questions.stem: This figure shows ciliated respiratory epithelium propelling material, including a trapped pathogen, upward toward the pharynx. A congenital defect in this ciliary function (e.g., primary ciliary dyskinesia) would predispose the patient to what?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recurrent respiratory tract infections from impaired mucociliary clearance

explanation.summary: The mucociliary escalator is an innate physical defense: cilia beat in a coordinated fashion to sweep mucus-trapped microbes out of the airways. Defective cilia (as in primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener syndrome) cause mucus stasis and recurrent sinopulmonary infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mucociliary escalator is an innate physical defense: cilia beat in a coordinated fashion to sweep mucus-trapped microbes out of the airways. Defective cilia (as in primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener syndrome) cause mucus stasis and recurrent sinopulmonary infections.

questions.stem: In the progression shown, septic shock is defined by hypotension that persists despite adequate IV fluid resuscitation. What is the primary mechanism of this refractory hypotension?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Widespread inflammatory-mediator-induced vasodilation (e.g., nitric oxide) with capillary leak

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pump failure from a large myocardial infarction

explanation.summary: Sepsis triggers systemic release of inflammatory mediators (TNF, IL-1, nitric oxide) causing profound vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. The resulting distributive shock does not correct with fluids alone and requires vasopressors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sepsis triggers systemic release of inflammatory mediators (TNF, IL-1, nitric oxide) causing profound vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. The resulting distributive shock does not correct with fluids alone and requires vasopressors.

questions.stem: In this sequence of acute inflammation, step 6 shows leukocytes leaving the vessel and migrating into tissue. Which molecules mediate the initial rolling of leukocytes along the endothelium?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Selectins (E- and P-selectin binding sialyl-Lewis X)

explanation.summary: Leukocyte extravasation proceeds through selectin-mediated rolling, chemokine-triggered integrin activation, firm adhesion (integrin-ICAM), and transmigration. Earlier steps show sentinel-cell mediators and increased vascular permeability that set the stage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukocyte extravasation proceeds through selectin-mediated rolling, chemokine-triggered integrin activation, firm adhesion (integrin-ICAM), and transmigration. Earlier steps show sentinel-cell mediators and increased vascular permeability that set the stage.

questions.stem: An IgG-coated target cell is bound by an NK cell through its CD16 (Fc-gamma) receptor and then killed. What is this killing mechanism called?

explanation.summary: In ADCC, IgG coats a target cell and its Fc region is recognized by CD16 (Fc-gamma-RIII) on NK cells, triggering perforin/granzyme release. This mechanism also contributes to the action of certain therapeutic monoclonal antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ADCC, IgG coats a target cell and its Fc region is recognized by CD16 (Fc-gamma-RIII) on NK cells, triggering perforin/granzyme release. This mechanism also contributes to the action of certain therapeutic monoclonal antibodies.

questions.stem: Several Toll-like receptors in this diagram sit within endosomes rather than on the cell surface. What class of pathogen-associated molecule do these endosomal TLRs primarily detect?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microbial and viral nucleic acids (ssRNA, dsRNA, CpG DNA)

explanation.summary: Endosomal TLR-3 (dsRNA), TLR-7 (ssRNA), and TLR-9 (unmethylated CpG DNA) sense nucleic acids from ingested microbes and viruses, driving IRF-dependent type I interferon and NF-kB-dependent inflammatory cytokines. Surface TLR-4/2/5 detect LPS, peptidoglycan/lipopeptides, and flagellin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Endosomal TLR-3 (dsRNA), TLR-7 (ssRNA), and TLR-9 (unmethylated CpG DNA) sense nucleic acids from ingested microbes and viruses, driving IRF-dependent type I interferon and NF-kB-dependent inflammatory cytokines. Surface TLR-4/2/5 detect LPS, peptidoglycan/lipopeptides, and flagellin.

questions.stem: This cartoon jokes that neutrophils can 'shoot traps' to catch pathogens. What is the actual name of this antimicrobial process?

explanation.summary: Neutrophils extrude webs of decondensed chromatin (DNA) studded with antimicrobial proteins such as myeloperoxidase and elastase that trap and kill extracellular microbes. This process is called NETosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils extrude webs of decondensed chromatin (DNA) studded with antimicrobial proteins such as myeloperoxidase and elastase that trap and kill extracellular microbes. This process is called NETosis.

questions.stem: These cultured cells display long, thin cytoplasmic veils/processes and are the most potent activators of naive T cells. What cell type are they?

explanation.summary: Dendritic cells extend numerous membrane processes that increase surface area for antigen capture and presentation. They are the principal professional antigen-presenting cells that prime naive T lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dendritic cells extend numerous membrane processes that increase surface area for antigen capture and presentation. They are the principal professional antigen-presenting cells that prime naive T lymphocytes.

questions.stem: The IL-12 / IFN-gamma feedback loop shown between a T cell and a macrophage is essential for eliminating which type of pathogen?

explanation.summary: Macrophage-derived IL-12 drives Th1 (and NK) cells to secrete IFN-gamma, which classically activates macrophages to kill phagocytosed intracellular organisms. Defects in this axis (e.g., IL-12 or IFN-gamma receptor mutations) cause susceptibility to mycobacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrophage-derived IL-12 drives Th1 (and NK) cells to secrete IFN-gamma, which classically activates macrophages to kill phagocytosed intracellular organisms. Defects in this axis (e.g., IL-12 or IFN-gamma receptor mutations) cause susceptibility to mycobacteria.

questions.stem: Identify the predominant white blood cells in this smear: cells with a multilobed (3-5 lobe) nucleus and pale, finely granular cytoplasm.

explanation.summary: Segmented neutrophils have a nucleus of 3-5 lobes joined by thin strands and neutral (pale) cytoplasmic granules. They are the most abundant circulating leukocyte and the first responders in acute bacterial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Segmented neutrophils have a nucleus of 3-5 lobes joined by thin strands and neutral (pale) cytoplasmic granules. They are the most abundant circulating leukocyte and the first responders in acute bacterial infection.

questions.stem: In the lectin pathway shown, mannose-binding lectin uses MASP-2 to cleave C4 and C2. MASP-2 is functionally analogous to which component of the classical pathway?

explanation.summary: The lectin pathway mirrors the classical pathway: MBL replaces C1q, and MASP-2 performs the C4/C2-cleaving protease role of C1r/C1s, generating the same C3 convertase (C4b2b) without requiring antibody.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lectin pathway mirrors the classical pathway: MBL replaces C1q, and MASP-2 performs the C4/C2-cleaving protease role of C1r/C1s, generating the same C3 convertase (C4b2b) without requiring antibody.

questions.stem: Unlike the other complement pathways, the alternative pathway shown does not require antibody or lectin binding. How is it initiated on a microbial surface?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spontaneous low-level hydrolysis of C3 ('C3 tickover') that deposits C3b on the microbe

explanation.summary: C3 continuously undergoes spontaneous hydrolysis ('tickover'). C3b deposited on a foreign surface binds factor B, which factor D cleaves to form C3bBb, stabilized by properdin. Host surfaces are protected by regulatory proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: C3 continuously undergoes spontaneous hydrolysis ('tickover'). C3b deposited on a foreign surface binds factor B, which factor D cleaves to form C3bBb, stabilized by properdin. Host surfaces are protected by regulatory proteins.

questions.stem: All three complement pathways in this schematic converge on C3 convertase and then a shared terminal pathway (C5-C9). What lytic structure does this terminal pathway assemble?

explanation.summary: After C5 is cleaved, C5b recruits C6, C7, C8, and multiple C9 molecules to form the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), a pore that osmotically lyses the target cell. This is the shared terminal step of all three pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: After C5 is cleaved, C5b recruits C6, C7, C8, and multiple C9 molecules to form the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), a pore that osmotically lyses the target cell. This is the shared terminal step of all three pathways.

questions.stem: This figure depicts a numbered sequence beginning with a barrier break and microbial entry, followed by sentinel-cell activation, secretion of mediators, increased vascular permeability, and leukocyte recruitment. Which vascular change occurring at step 4 is directly responsible for the local swelling (edema) seen clinically?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vasoconstriction reducing blood flow to the site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased vascular permeability allowing fluid and plasma proteins into tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet plug formation sealing the capillary

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased hydrostatic pressure within the venule

explanation.summary: The figure illustrates the acute inflammatory response. Mediators released by sentinel cells (step 3) act on the capillary-venule to increase vascular permeability (step 4), letting fluid, complement, and antibodies exit into tissue, which produces edema and delivers plasma proteins to the infection. Vasodilation (not vasoconstriction) increases flow, and the endothelium remains viable.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure illustrates the acute inflammatory response. Mediators released by sentinel cells (step 3) act on the capillary-venule to increase vascular permeability (step 4), letting fluid, complement, and antibodies exit into tissue, which produces edema and delivers plasma proteins to the infection. Vasodilation (not vasoconstriction) increases flow, and the endothelium remains viable.

questions.stem: This figure shows the three sequential steps by which a neutrophil leaves the bloodstream at a site of tissue injury: rolling, firm binding, and transmigration between endothelial cells. A child with recurrent bacterial infections without pus, delayed umbilical cord separation, and markedly elevated blood neutrophils has a defect in the molecule mediating the firm-binding step. Which molecule is defective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sialyl-Lewis X glycoprotein on the leukocyte

explanation.summary: The figure shows the leukocyte adhesion cascade: selectins mediate rolling, leukocyte CD11/CD18 integrins binding endothelial ICAM-1 mediate firm arrest, and PECAM-1 mediates diapedesis. Defective CD18 (beta-2 integrin) causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, characterized by recurrent infections without pus, delayed cord separation, and neutrophilia because neutrophils cannot firmly adhere and exit vessels. A Sialyl-Lewis X defect causes LAD type 2, which lacks the cord-separation delay severity and neutrophilia is less pronounced.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure shows the leukocyte adhesion cascade: selectins mediate rolling, leukocyte CD11/CD18 integrins binding endothelial ICAM-1 mediate firm arrest, and PECAM-1 mediates diapedesis. Defective CD18 (beta-2 integrin) causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, characterized by recurrent infections without pus, delayed cord separation, and neutrophilia because neutrophils cannot firmly adhere and exit vessels. A Sialyl-Lewis X defect causes LAD type 2, which lacks the cord-separation delay severity and neutrophilia is less pronounced.

questions.stem: This map shows the organization of the human MHC (HLA) gene complex, including the class I loci, class II loci, and intervening genes encoding complement components and TNF. On which chromosome is this gene complex located?

explanation.summary: The human HLA complex resides on the short arm of chromosome 6. The map shows class I genes (HLA-A, -B, -C), class II genes (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR) along with DM and the antigen-processing TAP/proteasome genes, and the class III region encoding complement proteins (C4, C2, factor B) and cytokines (TNF, lymphotoxin). Chromosome 14 carries the Ig heavy chain and TCR alpha loci, not the MHC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The human HLA complex resides on the short arm of chromosome 6. The map shows class I genes (HLA-A, -B, -C), class II genes (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR) along with DM and the antigen-processing TAP/proteasome genes, and the class III region encoding complement proteins (C4, C2, factor B) and cytokines (TNF, lymphotoxin). Chromosome 14 carries the Ig heavy chain and TCR alpha loci, not the MHC.

questions.stem: This figure shows three effector functions of antibodies: coating bacteria to promote uptake by a macrophage; blocking a microbe from attaching to epithelial cells; and depositing C3b/forming a membrane attack complex. The membrane attack complex generated in the right-hand panel kills the target microbe by which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking the microbe's adhesion to host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-linking Fc receptors to trigger degranulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Triggering caspase-mediated apoptosis of the microbe

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forming a transmembrane pore that causes osmotic lysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enhancing antigen presentation on MHC class I

explanation.summary: The panels show opsonization, neutralization, and complement activation. Antibody-triggered classical complement activation deposits C3b (an opsonin) and assembles the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), which inserts into the microbial membrane forming a pore. The resulting loss of osmotic integrity causes lysis. Neutralization (blocking adhesion) and opsonization are the other, distinct functions shown.
explanation.whyCorrect: The panels show opsonization, neutralization, and complement activation. Antibody-triggered classical complement activation deposits C3b (an opsonin) and assembles the membrane attack complex (C5b-9), which inserts into the microbial membrane forming a pore. The resulting loss of osmotic integrity causes lysis. Neutralization (blocking adhesion) and opsonization are the other, distinct functions shown.

questions.stem: This figure depicts the reaction occurring in the germinal center, showing B cells proliferating in a dark zone, being selected for improved affinity in a light zone by follicular dendritic cells and Tfh cells, and finally exiting as plasma cells and memory B cells. Which two processes occurring here improve antibody affinity and change antibody isotype, respectively?

explanation.summary: The germinal center is where affinity maturation and isotype switching occur. Somatic hypermutation introduces mutations into variable regions; high-affinity clones are selected by competing for antigen on follicular dendritic cells and for Tfh help. Class-switch recombination changes the heavy-chain constant region (e.g., IgM to IgG/IgA/IgE) without altering specificity. Both depend on activation-induced cytidine deaminase and yield plasma cells and memory B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The germinal center is where affinity maturation and isotype switching occur. Somatic hypermutation introduces mutations into variable regions; high-affinity clones are selected by competing for antigen on follicular dendritic cells and for Tfh help. Class-switch recombination changes the heavy-chain constant region (e.g., IgM to IgG/IgA/IgE) without altering specificity. Both depend on activation-induced cytidine deaminase and yield plasma cells and memory B cells.

questions.stem: This figure shows a dendritic cell activating a naive T cell, providing both TCR-MHC engagement and a costimulatory interaction. If the naive T cell receives the TCR-MHC signal (signal 1) but the costimulatory signal (signal 2) is absent, what is the usual consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The T cell lyses the dendritic cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: The T cell secretes maximal IL-2 and expands

choices.label: C
choices.text: The T cell is fully activated and proliferates normally

choices.label: D
choices.text: The T cell becomes anergic (functionally unresponsive)

choices.label: E
choices.text: The T cell differentiates directly into a memory cell

explanation.summary: Full activation of a naive T cell requires signal 1 (TCR recognition of peptide-MHC, shown with CD4/CD8 coreceptors) plus signal 2, costimulation via CD28 binding B7 (CD80/CD86) on the dendritic cell. If a T cell recognizes antigen without adequate costimulation, it is rendered anergic (or is deleted), a key mechanism of peripheral tolerance that prevents inappropriate activation against self-antigens presented in the absence of danger signals.
explanation.whyCorrect: Full activation of a naive T cell requires signal 1 (TCR recognition of peptide-MHC, shown with CD4/CD8 coreceptors) plus signal 2, costimulation via CD28 binding B7 (CD80/CD86) on the dendritic cell. If a T cell recognizes antigen without adequate costimulation, it is rendered anergic (or is deleted), a key mechanism of peripheral tolerance that prevents inappropriate activation against self-antigens presented in the absence of danger signals.

questions.stem: This figure shows a naive CD4+ T cell differentiating into distinct helper subsets depending on the cytokine environment, each producing characteristic effector cytokines and functions. Which subset, driven by IL-12 and secreting IFN-gamma, is most important for enhancing macrophage killing of intracellular bacteria?

explanation.summary: IL-12 (with IFN-gamma) drives Th1 differentiation; Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill ingested intracellular pathogens and promotes B-cell switching to opsonizing IgG. Th2 (IL-4) targets helminths and drives IgE; Th17 (IL-6, TGF-beta, IL-1) recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi; Treg (TGF-beta, IL-2) suppresses responses and maintains tolerance.
explanation.whyCorrect: IL-12 (with IFN-gamma) drives Th1 differentiation; Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill ingested intracellular pathogens and promotes B-cell switching to opsonizing IgG. Th2 (IL-4) targets helminths and drives IgE; Th17 (IL-6, TGF-beta, IL-1) recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi; Treg (TGF-beta, IL-2) suppresses responses and maintains tolerance.
